narrative:
The model estimated a 51% chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above an even split, but because your law-school application was assessed on this risk, it was enough to lead to rejection rather than admission.

The strongest factor behind that result was your LSAT score. At 24, it is well below the average of about 37 among accepted students, and it was the single most influential factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.30 was slightly above the accepted-student average of 3.23, and it was the second-most influential factor; it pushed toward passing. Your third-year class rank was also a positive influence: being in the fourth decile was below the accepted average near the sixth decile, but relative to the other information it still leaned toward passing. Thus, although two of the three leading factors worked in your favor, the LSAT result outweighed them enough to produce a narrow failure prediction.

To strengthen a future application, focus first on raising your LSAT score through structured preparation and, if feasible, a retake. Meet with admissions advisers to discuss how your part-time status and family-income context affected your record, and ask whether additional coursework, a stronger recent academic record, or a later application cycle would better demonstrate readiness for the bar.
